items.title: Mary Peltola Defeats Incumbent Republican in Alaska Senate Race
items.standfirst: Democratic challenger Mary Peltola triumphed over Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, rounding out a controversy-plagued race and handing the Democratic caucus a 56-44 majority in the Senate.
items.content: Mary Peltola speaks during a midterm election night party in Anchorage, Alaska, on Nov. 3, 2026. —Charly Triballeau—Getty ImagesDemocratic challenger Mary Peltola has defeated incumbent Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan in Alaska, rounding out one of the tightest and most controversial races of the midterm elections, and marking another notable GOP loss in what is typically a reliably red state.The Associated Press called the race on Tuesday evening, two weeks after Election Day, with Peltola securing 50.1% of the votes against Sullivan’s 45.8%. Peltola is the first Democrat elected to the Senate in Alaska since 2008. Trump won the state by 13 points in the 2024 presidential election.Peltola, a Yup'ik Alaska Native, served one term in the House of Representatives from 2022 to 2025 and became the first Alaska Native member of Congress and the first woman to represent Alaska in the lower chamber. She’ll now be the first Alaska Native in the Senate.Read More: The Candidates Who Made History in the MidtermsThe Alaska race is the last U.S. Senate contest to be called, partly due to the razor-thin margin between Peltola and Sullivan, but also because Alaska has a 15-day grace period after Election Day for mailed ballots to be returned to the elections office and counted. The state uses a ranked-choice voting system, which can make the process of certifying votes more complicated and would have resulted in a second round of vote tabulating if the leading candidate had received less than 50% of the first-round votes cast.Peltola posted on social media following the election call that “there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first. Thank you, Alaska. Let’s get to work.”Her victory puts the Senate balance of power at 56-44, in favor of Democrats, who secured control of both chambers of Congress in the midterms as the American public appeared to reject President Donald Trump amid concerns about the Iran war, inflation, and more. In the eight Senate contests that appeared least predictable, Democrats won all of them, and they even won in Mississippi too, where election forecasters had rated the race as likely Republican.Read More: The Democratic Wins No Election Forecaster ExpectedThe race was dominated by controversy over allegations that independent runner Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, was a spoiler candidate, intended to confuse Alaskans and draw votes away from the incumbent Republican Senator with the same first and last name.Despite protests from Trump, Republicans were unsuccessful in trying to remove the second Sullivan from the ballot. A federal judge on Nov. 1 dismissed a lawsuit by the Trump Administration that sought to delay certifying the results in Alaska if the incumbent Republican lost the race. "The United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified 'investigation' of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy,” ruled District Judge Sharon Gleason, referring to the Oct. 22 lawsuit. The New York Times on Oct. 28 reported that “operatives” aligned with Peltola had “spent months recruiting candidates to peel votes from Senator Dan Sullivan.” Peltola vehemently denied the claims.Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, launched a probe into the matter on Oct. 29, to investigate what he alleged to be an “organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections.” On Election Day, Sen. Sullivan said “people are disgusted by what has gone down in Alaska” and alleged that America was “witnessing the biggest election cheating scandal in the history of the state of Alaska.” Peltola described the noise around the double Sullivan controversy as “just another distraction,” dismissing it as “stuff to sell newspapers, stuff to get subscriptions.”Amid the fallout, Peltola’s campaign sued Alaska in an effort to obtain the records on rejected absentee ballots. The lawsuit, filed Nov. 6, argued the failure to release the records would amount to “severely prejudicing [Peltola’s] ability to monitor Alaska’s election certification process to make sure that all ballots are counted according to law.” Alaska Superior Court Judge Thomas Matthews ruled against the campaign’s request on Nov. 11, stipulating that the records “cannot reasonably be produced at this juncture, nor redacted of confidential information.”Trump, meanwhile, accused Peltola of “perpetrating such a terrible scheme” and argued that incumbent Sen. Sullivan should be prematurely announced as winner, even as Peltola inched slightly ahead in the counted votes. In a Truth Social post on Nov. 5, Trump said that the votes for Dan J. Sullivan, as well as those for Gerald Heikes, a GOP runner and the fourth candidate on Alaska’s ballot, should be “given to the REAL Dan Sullivan” insisting there is “no other fair solution.” Trump doubled down on his argument on Nov. 7, claiming that if all those votes were combined, then the Alaska race would be “over” and the incumbent Senator would be announced as the winner.Aside from the controversy which dominated much of the discourse around the race, Peltola and Sullivan also clashed over proposals to build data centers in Alaska, an issue felt nationwide.When asked about data centers, Peltola said she takes her “cue from the people of that region,” deferring to local support, provided it doesn’t strain the grid for existing ratepayers. Whereas Sullivan has pushed to bring data centers onto Alaska’s Air Force and joint military installations.Peltola also hit out at Sullivan for continuing to support Trump’s war with Iran, which remains deeply unpopular with Americans, in part due to the financial ramifications of the conflict which has entered its ninth month. The disruption to the Strait of Hormuz, a vital trade route, has led to record high diesel prices.In an NBC exit poll carried out Nov. 3, more than 80% of voters said they were worried about the price of necessities including gas and diesel fuel, food and groceries, utilities and healthcare.

items.title: Mary Peltola unseats Sen. Dan Sullivan, giving Dems a 56-seat Senate majority
items.standfirst: It's the first time in 18 years a Democrat has won a Senate race in the state.
items.content: Former Rep. Mary Peltola ousted GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska — the first time in 18 years a Democrat has won a Senate race in the state.Her win gives Democrats a 56-44 edge in the Senate.Peltola was one of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s top recruits for the cycle. She overpowered a Republican rescue mission for Sullivan and allegations of misconduct against her from former staffers to flip a state President Donald Trump won by 13 points in 2024. Her victory continues the blue wave born from voters’ frustrations at high costs and the Trump administration.Peltola will return to Washington, where she will become the first Alaska Native to serve in the Senate after previously holding the same distinction in the House.Her campaign had projected confidence about her path to victory as the vote count dragged on in a far-flung, rural state with long grace periods for late-arriving ballots.But her win was not without tumult. Trump’s Department of Justice sued to try to stop the certification if Sullivan lost, claiming voters could be confused by his same-name challenger. The president went so far as to call for votes for retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan and another longshot candidate in the four-way, all-party contest to be transferred to the incumbent.The Justice Department also started probing efforts to recruit Dan J. Sullivan after a New York Times report suggesting members of Peltola’s campaign and Senate Democrats’ campaign arm were involved. Both had previously denied involvement.

items.title: What Is the Kerch Bridge—and Why Does Ukraine Keep Attacking It?
items.standfirst: The attack is a symbolic blow to Russian President Vladimir Putin ahead of a summit with U.S. President Donald Trump.
items.content: A picture taken on July 17, 2023, shows a Russian warship sailing near the Kerch bridge, which links the Russian mainland to Crimea, following an attack claimed by Ukrainian forces. —STRINGER––AFP/Getty ImagesAn overnight Ukrainian missile attack has severely damaged the vital Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia, delivering a symbolic blow to Russian President Vladimir Putin ahead of a summit in Asia where he is expected to meet President Donald Trump.The road and rail bridge was built after Russia invaded and annexed the Crimean peninsula in 2014 and connects Crimea to Russia's southern Krasnodar region.Ukrainian officials shared videos on social media that appeared to show a missile strike on the bridge and an entire section of the structure collapsing. TIME could not immediately verify the footage.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Tuesday morning that the overnight strikes served as a reminder to “Russia that war will always return to where it began.”Sergei Aksyonov, the Russian-installed governor of Crimea, confirmed the Ukrainian strike and said traffic across the bridge had been suspended.“Measures are being taken to restore transport links disrupted as a result of enemy attacks on the Crimean Bridge,” he said Tuesday on Telegram.Ukraine's armed forces said the bridge's road arch had fallen into the Kerch Strait, which connects the Sea of Azov with the Black Sea, while the railway arch had also sustained damage.“For the occupiers, this is more than a symbolic blow. The bridge was the main artery carrying fuel, ammunition, equipment and personnel to the peninsula and on into southern Ukraine,” the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said, framing the attack as an effort to disrupt Russian military supply lines. “The occupiers are left with fewer and fewer land routes to Crimea. Every hour without traffic over the bridge means Russian groupings in the south receive less of what they need to keep fighting.”Zelensky added that the attack was part of “an unprecedented operation in response to Russian strikes on our infrastructure.”Russia has been ramping up its attacks on Ukraine's civilian and energy infrastructure as the country heads into the winter months, placing further pressure on Kyiv amid ongoing peace negotiations.In the Ukrainian capital, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said Russian forces had struck two bridges spanning the Dnipro River and other infrastructure on Monday.Officials in Kyiv also reported further strikes on the country's power grid across multiple regions, as cities throughout Ukraine faced water and electricity outages.Ukraine, meanwhile, has intensified its own military pressure on Russia, with the attack on the Kerch Bridge coming amid the largest overnight Ukrainian drone barrage against Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022. Russia's Defense Ministry confirmed it had shot down 1,441 drones across 22 regions.Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday that Russian Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin had briefed Putin on the situation at the Crimean Bridge, according to Russian news agency Interfax. "There is no doubt that the bridge will be restored and will be even better than before,” Peskov added.This combination of pictures shows (bottom) a grab taken from a video released on Nov. 17, 2026, by the Ukrainian Security Service showing the damaged after a strike on Crimean bridge (Kerch bridge) and (top) a view of the bridge taken Oct. 14, 2022. —Ukrainian Security Service––AFP PHOTO/Getty ImagesWhy the Kerch bridge matters to PutinThe Kerch bridge, also known as the Crimean bridge, stretches roughly 19 km (12 miles) across the strait, providing a direct road and rail link between Crimea and Russia without the need to travel through mainland Ukraine.Carlo Masala, a professor of security and defense policy at the Bundeswehr University Munich, describes it as one of “Putin's prestige projects after he annexed Crimea.”“It's a highly symbolic and high value target for the Ukrainians to destroy the bridge," he tells TIME.Putin personally drove the lead truck across the bridge when its road section opened in 2018 and also attended the launch of passenger rail services in 2019, underscoring the political importance he has placed on the crossing.“Symbolically, the bridge is one of the clearest physical expressions of Moscow’s claim to Crimea,” Basil Germond, a professor of international security at Lancaster University, tells TIME.Germond explains that the bridge “was intended to demonstrate that Crimea had been permanently integrated into Russia.""Serious damage to such a prominent and heavily defended structure is therefore an embarrassing blow to the Kremlin," he says.The bridge has repeatedly been targeted by Ukraine since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. Ukrainian officials have previously described an attack involving explosives carried by a truck in 2022, attacks using naval surface drones in 2023, and a further operation involving underwater explosions in 2025.Beyond its symbolic importance, experts tell TIME that the latest strike also demonstrates Ukraine's military capabilities and its ability to target Russian infrastructure.“What Ukrainians showed is that they now have ballistic missiles which can hit targets in Russia very precisely within a reach of thousands of kilometers,” says Masala.The damage could also have broader consequences for Russia, with the bridge serving as an important transport link for civilians traveling between Crimea and the Russian mainland.“If the road crossing remains closed, this may also deepen the feeling among residents of Crimea that the peninsula is geographically vulnerable rather than securely connected to Russia. All that plays a part in diminishing morale among the Russian population,” explains Germond.The disruption could also complicate Russian military supply lines, although Moscow has developed alternative routes to support its forces in southern Ukraine.Germond says that “operationally, disruption to the road bridge will make Russian logistics more complicated and expensive.”“Russia can still use the occupied land corridor through southern Ukraine, as well as ferries and other connections, but these alternatives are longer, less efficient and potentially more exposed to Ukrainian attack,” he adds.The apparent obstruction of the shipping channel beneath the bridge could create an additional challenge for maritime traffic between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.The strike has nevertheless been welcomed by some Ukrainian observers, who celebrated the long-awaited destruction of parts of the bridge. Serhii Sternenko, a former adviser to Ukraine's Defense Ministry, wrote on social media: “Ukraine destroyed [the] Crimean bridge. Just help Ukraine defeat Russia. We can do it.”Still, experts caution that the destruction of the bridge is little more than symbolic.“The strike does not in itself transform the balance of power or guarantee Ukraine a stronger negotiating position. It does, however, reinforce Kyiv’s argument that Ukraine is not a defeated or passive actor. Ukraine has demonstrated that it can penetrate Russian defenses, strike strategically and politically important infrastructure, and impose costs far beyond the immediate front line,” says Germond.How could the strike affect Ukraine-Russia peace talks?The latest blow to the Kremlin comes as Putin prepares to travel to China for a trilateral meeting with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.Although the full agenda for the meeting remains unclear, Putin has previously indicated that it would include discussions on ending the war in Ukraine, with Trump telling reporters Monday that the topics would range from denuclearization to Iran and Ukraine.“I think [Putin]’s backing down a little bit. I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher,” Trump said, adding “I think he'd like to see it finished.”Germond argues that the strike on Kerch is an important display of Ukraine's military capabilities ahead of the diplomatic summit, reinforcing Kyiv's position that it can continue to impose costs on Russia despite ongoing negotiations.“Ukraine will want to persuade Trump and other international partners that continued support strengthens a capable actor that still has meaningful leverage. Kyiv’s message is that negotiations conducted under sustained pressure on Russia are more likely to produce results than negotiations based on the assumption that Russian military superiority is inevitable,” he says.The ongoing peace efforts have been led by U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who met with Putin in Moscow last week before traveling to Ireland later that day to brief Zelensky on the developments.Their visit followed two days of U.S.-mediated negotiations in Abu Dhabi between Russian and Ukrainian delegations. Those discussions ended without a major breakthrough, with significant differences remaining between the two sides.Kushner confirmed Monday that the U.S. remained in communication with Ukrainian and European officials, with European representatives expected to be included in the next round of talks.“Important challenges remain, and a final agreement will require difficult decisions. But we are making progress, in close coordination with Russia, Ukraine, and Europe, toward an outcome that can end this war, strengthen European security, and create the foundations for lasting peace,” he said.

items.title: The U.S. Has Lost Its Measles-Elimination Status. Here’s What That Means
items.standfirst: After more than a year of continuous measles transmission, the U.S. has lost a public-health milestone it held for more than two decades.
items.content: For more than a quarter of a century, the U.S. has held measles-elimination status, meaning the virus was no longer spreading continuously within the country. Prior to the introduction of the first measles vaccine in 1963, nearly all American children contracted the disease before they were 15, for an annual case count of up to four million, including 400 to 500 deaths and 48,000 hospitalizations. But an aggressive vaccination campaign changed all of that, and measles was declared eliminated in the U.S. in 2000. No more.On Nov. 17, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) announced that the U.S. had lost that status after at least 12 months of uninterrupted transmission. Falling vaccination rates—fueled in part by antivaccine misinformation spread by a vocal community that includes Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)—have allowed the virus, contained for more than a generation, to spread widely. As of Nov. 12, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) had recorded 5,412 measles cases in the U.S. in 2026: 5,394 reported by 47 jurisdictions, plus 18 cases among international visitors. That case count is more than twice the 2,289 cases reported in all of 2025, including three deaths—the highest caseload since 1991—and is 19 times greater than the 285 cases in 2024.“It's a tremendous step backwards for public health in the United States,” says Dr. Paul Offit, attending physician in the Division of Infectious Diseases at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia. “But, in some ways, the ruling is irrelevant. Measles has now established a foothold in this country. It's endemic.”As with so much else in the field of epidemiology, the standards that must be met to gain or lose elimination status for measles aren't entirely straightforward. For one thing, elimination doesn’t mean zero cases. Measles can still be brought into the country by travelers and spread among people who aren’t protected.Even cases that appear to have a domestic origin are not necessarily enough to cost a country its elimination status. PAHO considers measles transmission re-established when the same virus genotype and lineage circulate uninterrupted in a country for at least 12 months. In the U.S., the outbreak began on Jan. 20, 2025, and reached that threshold a year later, according to PAHO. Genome sequencing helps scientists identify the genotype and lineage of the virus in a case and determine whether it is linked to an ongoing chain of transmission. In August, Utah health officials published a preprint study documenting sustained transmission in the state. The PAHO commission reviewed the evidence from across the country before determining that the U.S. had lost its elimination status. In 2026 so far, the CDC has reported 43 new outbreaks nationwide, nearly matching the 48 reported in all of 2025.Vaccination rates don’t have to fall much for outbreaks to take hold, especially in communities with pockets of low coverage. PAHO says communities should aim for at least 95% coverage with both doses of the measles vaccine to help prevent transmission. High vaccination coverage also helps protect people who can’t be vaccinated, including infants too young to receive the vaccine and people with certain medical conditions. MMR vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners fell from 95.2% in the 2019–2020 school year to 92.4% in 2025–2026, according to the CDC.“It’s so tragic that we’ve allowed measles to return to America,” says Dr. Peter Hotez, co-director of Texas Children’s Hospital Center for Vaccine Development. “In the prevaccine era, measles exhibited a distinctive seasonality in late winter [and] early spring. This same pattern has recurred in 2025 and 2026, so the prediction is we will [see] an even larger surge at that time in 2027.”What makes things worse is that while measles is an easy illness to prevent—two doses of the MMR vaccine reduce the risk of contracting the disease by 97%—it is wildly easy to catch and spread. An unvaccinated person who comes into contact with someone with measles has a 90% chance of becoming infected, according to Johns Hopkins Medicine, and the virus can linger on surfaces or in the air for up to two hours after an infected person has left a room. What’s more, people who are infected with the virus can be stealth carriers before they even know they’re sick. According to the World Health Organization, the virus can spread for up to four days before the disease’s characteristic rash appears and four more days after it has faded.And the disease can lead to serious, sometimes fatal complications. “Measles is one of the most contagious diseases in the world,” said Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO, at a Nov. 17 press conference. “It can cause pneumonia, encephalitis, blindness, and even death.”The U.S. is not alone in battling a measles resurgence; the problem extends across the Americas. In Nov. 2025, Canada lost its elimination status following an outbreak that began in Oct. 2024, spread across 10 provinces and the Northwest Territories, and lasted more than a year. Mexico and Bolivia also lost their elimination status on Nov. 17. In these countries, as in the U.S., gaps in vaccination coverage have helped fuel outbreaks.Regaining America’s lost measles-elimination status won’t be easy. Kennedy’s continued questioning of public-health authorities could complicate efforts to rebuild trust in vaccination. In August, he went so far as to speculate, in a post on X, that the announcement by Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro of two measles-related deaths in the state “may even have been altogether fabricated by one of the Governor's hopeful staffers.”Regaining elimination status will require interrupting endemic transmission for at least 12 months, documenting that progress, and strengthening vaccination, surveillance, and outbreak response.“Measles elimination is not a trophy that is won once and placed on a shelf,” Barbosa said at the Nov. 17 press conference. “It is an achievement that must be safeguarded every day.”Adds Offit: “We will be dealing with measles this year and next year and the year after that, until we get our immunization rates up.”

clusters.title: U.S. Strikes Qeshm Island as Vance Says Iran Won’t Become ‘Forever War’
clusters.neutral_headline: U.S. Strikes Qeshm Island as Vance Says Iran Won’t Become ‘Forever War’
bullet_summary: Reported by Time Magazine, CBS News

items.title: U.S. Strikes Qeshm Island as Vance Says Iran Won’t Become ‘Forever War’
items.standfirst: The strikes came hours after Iran targeted a U.S. radar site in Bahrain, as an imminent diplomatic agreement to end the war has seemed unlikely.
items.content: Commercial vessels are seen anchored between Iranâs Qeshm and Larak islands amid disruptions to maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran on Sept. 11, 2026. —Fatemeh Bahrami—Anadolu/Getty ImagesThe U.S. and Iran exchanged attacks on Tuesday in the latest flare-up of the war that the Trump Administration promised would end after the U.S. midterms.American warplanes hit an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the crucial Strait of Hormuz waterway. An unnamed official speaking to CNN and other outlets called the strikes “self-defense” in response to alleged “aggression targeting American personnel and assets” by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.Iran had earlier attempted an attack on American military targets in Bahrain, which is home to the ​US Navy's Fifth Fleet. But the U.S. Central Command, which has jurisdiction in the Middle East, announced on social media that the Iranian one-way attack drones “were intercepted without any damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel.”Ahmad Nafisi, deputy governor of Iran’s southern Hormozgan province, also told state media Tuesday that the attacks on Qeshm “caused no damage to residential, commercial, or infrastructural areas.”Kuwait’s Armed Forces also announced early Wednesday morning that its air defenses were responding to “drone attacks.” Iran later took responsibility for attacks on Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem Air Base, which hosts U.S. forces.The latest flare-up resembled other recent skirmishes around the Strait of Hormuz. Washington has so far held back from resuming major hostilities with Tehran. Still, in the lead-up and the immediate wake of the U.S. midterm elections, Qeshm Island has become a major flashpoint, involving so-called “limited” strikes. On the eve of the midterms, the U.S. carried out an attack on the island, and Trump confirmed more strikes on Nov. 6.The Wall Street Journal reported on Nov. 2 that the U.S. had engaged in smaller-scale, unannounced strikes against Iran “for several weeks,” with unnamed officials describing them as defensive and preventative of an Iranian attack on commercial ships in the strait.The ​latest strikes came despite talks between Iran and mediators Oman ​and Qatar. An imminent diplomatic agreement to end the war has seemed unlikely. The U.S. has maintained its blockade on Iranian ports to cut off its oil exports and damage the Middle East nation’s economy. President Donald Trump also previously warned that full combat operations could continue if Iran refuses to heed the U.S.’s demands.“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump posted on his platform Truth Social on Nov. 12. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”Not a ‘forever war’Trump’s Vice President J.D. Vance said earlier this week that the Administration won’t let the conflict with Iran last and that it will wrap up long before they leave the White House in 2029. “[Trump] is not going to let this become a forever war,” Vance told Fox News on Monday. “And the people who want it to become a forever war, they can attack me all they want to, because we signed up to not do this. We told the American people we would do no more forever wars.”Vance, considered a possible contender for the 2028 presidential election, blamed the American public’s frustrations with the ongoing Iran war for the GOP’s massive losses to Democrats during the midterms. Vance had originally been tasked with leading peace negotiations with Iran, but Trump on Nov. 12 reassigned him to focus domestically on investigating fraud in Democratic-led jurisdictions.The U.S. appears to maintain its military might in the region, according to analysis by the Institute for National Security Studies in Israel; a third American aircraft carrier—the U.S.S. Theodore Roosevelt—arrived in the Middle East on Nov. 15. And Trump has warned that escalation by Iran would be responded to by the U.S. In Manila on Tuesday, the President said in response to questions regarding Iran reportedly developing plans to deploy a “dirty bomb” in Washington: “If there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before.”Trump is expected to hold a trilateral summit on Thursday in China with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, where the Iran war is on the agenda.

items.title: Democrats see an immigration opening despite Stephen Miller’s rise
items.standfirst: Several moderate Democrats have already placed calls to the White House and Trump administration officials to express a willingness to work together.
items.content: In the days before the midterm election, Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) felt confident that a blue wave could open the door to immigration reform.Cuellar was so bullish that he reached out to acting Immigration and Customs Enforcement director David Venturella and the Customs and Border Protection commissioner Rodney Scott to feel out areas of “common ground,” he said in an interview.Now Cuellar is one of several moderate Democrats angling to strike a deal with the White House, especially on reining in ICE officers and creating legal pathways to citizenship for some immigrants. They’re undeterred by President Donald Trump’s elevation of immigration hardliner Stephen Miller to chief of staff. And they’re buoyed by Trump’s recent admission that his deportations policy was “too tough.”Several of these Democrats have already placed calls to Trump and DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin to express a willingness to work together. Cuellar said he reached back out to Venturella and Scott after the election to try to schedule meetings.“If the president, as the president of the United States, makes a decision — and not a chief of staff — we can get the job done,” Cuellar said in an interview. “I’m sure we’re going to find a lot of differences, but if we sit down, we can definitely resolve them.”It’ll be a tough road: Securing buy-in from the White House becomes undoubtedly more complicated with Miller, a champion of the administration’s aggressive deportation push. Republicans in Congress have largely been willing to defer to the president on the issue. And Democratic leaders have questioned Trump’s sincerity and said they have no interest in working with Miller.The possibility will become even more tenuous once Democrats begin investigating the Trump administration, including the president’s immigration enforcement agencies.CBP and ICE did not respond to requests for comment.Neither did Democratic leaders Sen. Chuck Schumer and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries.Democrats like Cuellar, Sen.-elects James Talarico of Texas and Annie Andrews of South Carolina are aware of all of those hurdles. But they’re betting the midterms have created an opening for serious talks: Latino voters across the country swung hard back toward Democrats this cycle, and more and more Republicans are recognizing that their immigration agenda hurt them politically.Talarico and Andrews have publicly expressed interest in working with the president on immigration, and both ran on platforms that emphasized creating paths to citizenship for undocumented immigrants.“I’m ready to work with President Trump to fix this broken immigration system,” Talarico said in a statement.Inside the White House, there’s a recognition that the president will proceed however he so chooses, regardless of who the chief of staff is. Trump is accessible to outside voices — journalists, business leaders and lawmakers regularly call him directly — and often poses policy questions to aides and allies as he decides which direction he will go.“Everybody’s like, ‘Well, it’s never going to happen with Stephen Miller.’ Look, Donald Trump’s the president. I don’t care if Stephen Miller’s the chief of staff or Susie Wiles or John Kelly or whoever the chief of staff might be,” said a person close to the White House, granted anonymity to speak about the internal dynamic.For Democrats, there’s a real political incentive to getting a deal done ahead of a critical 2028 presidential election — especially as the party seeks to win back voter trust on immigration and border security, policy areas that spelled doom for them in 2024.“You have these Democrats who flip red states, and it’s also to their self-interest, right? Not just to do rhetoric, and go big or go home, but actually come to the middle with the president, with the Republicans. Because if not, I think that the big lesson this election is, Hispanic voters are gonna flip back ... if they don’t see Democrats delivering anything the next two years,” said Rebecca Shi, the executive director of ABIC, a coalition of pro-immigration reform business executives.She added that there’s a lesson for Republicans, too, if they don’t come to the table: “They will lose the White House.”White House spokesperson Lauren Bis touted Trump’s immigration accomplishments, including border security, a drop in crime and the creation of the Homeland Security Task Force and said the president’s “strong immigration policy remains unchanged.”She said Democrats should work alongside Trump to “keep our southern border secure, remove dangerous illegal criminals from our communities, and stop the illicit trafficking of lethal drugs.”Democrats welcomed the president’s remarks on 60 Minutes on Sunday, when he said he was open to legal pathways for some unauthorized immigrants who haven’t committed crimes and are working and contributing to the economy. Mullin also floated an openness to a bipartisan immigration overhaul involving DACA, which could provide permanent legal status to some undocumented immigrants who arrived in the U.S. as children, even as he — and the president — have insisted that any proposal wouldn’t include amnesty.In a sign that Democrats have learned the lessons of the Biden administration, many of them are eager to pair reforms with border security measures.Cuellar, who will chair the Homeland Security Appropriations subcommittee in the next conference, has long suggested including guardrails on ICE in the next funding bill, such as requiring judicial warrants, rolling out body camera usage and restoring “sensitive locations” such as churches and schools as off-limits.Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.), another Democrat who has expressed interest in working with the Trump administration, said that beyond “talk,” it would help to see some smaller concrete policy shifts from the White House to affirm that Trump is, in fact, open to changes to the immigration system.“The way to do that is to have some reforms already at ICE — whether it’s shutting down these detention centers, giving certain level of protections, whether to veterans, so they don't get deported, to maybe parents of U.S. citizens, they don’t get deported — something to show that, you know, it's not just talk, this isn’t going to be a policy led by Stephen Miller,” he said.But Miller remains a bogeyman for Democrats, someone they view as responsible for the president’s most extreme immigration policies. As chief of staff, he can ensure he’s one of the last people in the president’s ear — and that the White House doesn’t bend to what he sees as unrealistic Democratic demands.“The reason why they wouldn’t do an amnesty deal, I believe, is because it would be the ultimate and most public contradiction of the central thesis of this entire political program as it was sold to voters,” said Mike Howell, president of the Oversight Project and a member of the Mass Deportation Coalition. “It would be the end of the America First coalition as it currently exists.”Democrats' distrust of Miller will also make it challenging for them to align on any potential deal with the White House.“Stephen Miller is the mastermind and architect of terror, and death, and illegality in this country, and he is not anyone who even understands truthfully what immigration policy should look like,” said Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-Calif).“No deals, man. No deals,” she added.The White House pointed to Miller’s experience on the Hill as a valuable asset. White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said unlike Democrats “who refused to work with the President and blocked many of his popular policies, Stephen Miller has a track record of spearheading bipartisan efforts: public safety reform, making our cities such as Washington, D.C. and Memphis safe again, drug pricing transparency, and unleashing a nuclear energy renaissance.”Lawmakers are waiting for the president to make the first move.Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who will continue to lead his fellow Republicans when Democrats retake control of the Senate this January, told reporters after the election that “if there's something he wants to do there, we can have that conversation.”“There are always some landmines, which is why in the past the wheels have kind of come off, despite some really good efforts at trying to find a landing spot. But yeah we're open to something he wants to propose,” Thune added.Jordain Carney contributed to this report.

items.title: Protesters rally in downtown Manila to oppose President Trump's visit to the Philippines
items.standfirst: Thousands of people across the Philippines are protesting Donald Trump’s arrival for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila, the first stop on his Asia tour before traveling to China. Demonstrators cite concerns over U.S. foreign policy and the Pax Silica project, a U.S.-backed initiative aimed at developing an AI hub in the nation’s capital.

items.title: Hundreds arrested in anti-Trump protests in Philippines amid anger over Iran war and AI pact
items.standfirst: Organisers say up to 10,000 people could join next round of demonstrations as US president arrives for Asean summitAsean and Apec summits – as it happenedHundreds of people have been arrested in heated demonstrations against Donald Trump in Manila, as the US president arrived in the city for a leaders’ summit.Organisers claimed as many as 10,000 people would be joining protests against Trump in the capital of the Philippines on Tuesday, where he is attending the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit. The crowds were expected to try to march to the summit site. Continue reading...
